citation: Jacqueline Leybaert and Marie-Noëlle Van Cutsem. (2002). Counting in Sign Language. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1006/jecp.2002.2660
title: Belgian French Sign Language number-sign sequence as a base-5, rule-bound visuomanual counting system
description: The article describes Belgian French Sign Language's cardinal number signs as a single-handed, visuomanual system in which "BFSL number signs follows a consistent base-5 rule": from 1 to 5, 6 to 9, 11 to 15, and so on, one adds a finger for the next number, so number is inherently represented in each sign's finger configuration. Decade numbers are snapped configurations, and numbers within decades from 20 are concatenations of decade and unit signs. The article contrasts this with oral French, where the first 16 numbers are conventional and rule-bound structure begins later.
requirements: Learners must be exposed to the BFSL (or signed French) number-sign system, whose structure the article states is the same in signed French and Signed Coded Completed French
constraints: The base-5 structure holds for Belgian French Sign Language and American Sign Language but not for French Sign Language, and the concatenation rule does not apply to numbers between 11 and 19
target_learners: deaf children learning to count in sign language
hearing children learning oral number words
target_learning_goals: acquisition of the conventional number sequence
mapping linguistic counting onto numerosity representations
examples: The article details sign formation: 6 is the thumb alone moved twice, 7 adds the index finger, and 23 is the 20 sign followed by extension of three fingers
key_sources: Jacqueline Leybaert and Marie-Noëlle Van Cutsem. (2002). Counting in Sign Language. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1006/jecp.2002.2660

article_title: An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom
citation: Lisa Hasenbein, Ulrich Trautwein, Jens-Uwe Hahn, Stephan Soller, Richard Göllner. (2024). An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09646-4
title: Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect (BFLPE)
description: The Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect is the theoretical account that students' academic self-concept depends on the achievement level of their reference group: higher class-average achievement depresses self-concept at fixed individual achievement. As the article puts it, "two equally able students will evaluate themselves differently depending on the performance level of their classmates, whom they use as a reference for their self-evaluation." This study experimentally reproduces the effect in an IVR classroom and identifies students' perceived class performance level as the mediating mechanism.
requirements: A reference group of classmates whose performance-related behavior is visible to the student, so that social comparison information can be perceived
constraints: In this experiment the negative effect appeared only for situational self-concept and between the extreme conditions (20% vs. 80%), not for dispositional self-concept or moderate comparison standards
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept, self-evaluation of one's own abilities
examples: Virtual classmates who raised their hands in response to the teacher's questions served as the manipulated reference-group performance signal.
key_sources: Lisa Hasenbein, Ulrich Trautwein, Jens-Uwe Hahn, Stephan Soller, Richard Göllner. (2024). An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09646-4

article_title: The Big-fish–little-pond-effect Stands Up to Critical Scrutiny: Implications for Theory, Methodology, and Future Research
citation: Marsh, H. W., Seaton, M., Trautwein, U., Lüdtke, O., Hau, K. T., O'Mara, A. J., & Craven, R. G. (2008). The Big-fish–little-pond-effect Stands Up to Critical Scrutiny: Implications for Theory, Methodology, and Future Research. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9075-6
title: The BFLPE theoretical model: frame-of-reference effects on academic self-concept
description: The BFLPE model holds that students evaluate their academic accomplishments against the average ability level of others in their school, so the same objective ability produces different academic self-concepts depending on the school's average ability. Marsh formulated this as an educational application of frame-of-reference and psychophysical judgment research. The model generates seven predictions, including that "school-average ability will be negatively related to ASC after controlling for individual student ability" and that all students in a high-ability school would have lower ASCs than they would in a low-ability school, with small or non-significant interactions between school-average and individual ability.
requirements: Testing requires a multilevel design with many schools, an objective achievement measure comparable across schools, an appropriate ASC measure, and tests of school-average achievement effects controlling for individual achievement
constraints: The model operationalizes the standard of comparison as school-average ability and makes no predictions about the relative importance of school versus class frames of reference
examples: Marsh (1984a) operationalized the standard of comparison as school-average ability; the model predicts a below-average ASC for an average-ability student attending a high-ability school
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Seaton, M., Trautwein, U., Lüdtke, O., Hau, K. T., O'Mara, A. J., & Craven, R. G. (2008). The Big-fish–little-pond-effect Stands Up to Critical Scrutiny: Implications for Theory, Methodology, and Future Research. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9075-6

article_title: The Big-fish–little-pond-effect Stands Up to Critical Scrutiny: Implications for Theory, Methodology, and Future Research
citation: Marsh, H. W., Seaton, M., Trautwein, U., Lüdtke, O., Hau, K. T., O'Mara, A. J., & Craven, R. G. (2008). The Big-fish–little-pond-effect Stands Up to Critical Scrutiny: Implications for Theory, Methodology, and Future Research. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9075-6
title: School organization policies (tracking, ability grouping, selective schools, gifted programs) should account for the negative BFLPE on academic self-concept
description: Because academic self-concept predicts future achievement, coursework selection, and educational attainment, the BFLPE carries policy implications for how schools are organized. The article states the results "have important implications for the way in which schools are organized (e.g., tracking, ability grouping, academically selective schools, and gifted education programs)" — grouping high-ability students together imposes a more demanding frame of reference that lowers each student's academic self-concept. Planners should weigh these self-concept costs against any achievement benefits of such arrangements.
requirements: Decisions about ability grouping or selective schooling should be evaluated with the BFLPE evidence on academic self-concept in view, since ASC predicts future achievement and educational attainment
constraints: The article notes the achievement effects of tracking itself are near zero (Hattie's meta-analytic average effect size = 0.05), and it treats gifted programs as distinct from high-ability tracks
target_learners: school students, particularly those in or being considered for tracked, selective, or gifted education settings
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept, coursework selection, educational attainment
examples: The article cites the BFLPE's robustness across countries and long-term follow-ups as the basis for its policy relevance to tracking, ability grouping, selective schools, and gifted education programs
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Seaton, M., Trautwein, U., Lüdtke, O., Hau, K. T., O'Mara, A. J., & Craven, R. G. (2008). The Big-fish–little-pond-effect Stands Up to Critical Scrutiny: Implications for Theory, Methodology, and Future Research. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9075-6

article_title: Disentangling the Long-Term Compositional Effects of School-Average Achievement and SES: a Substantive-Methodological Synergy
citation: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Dicke, T., Guo, J., Parker, P. D., & Basarkod, G. (2023). Disentangling the Long-Term Compositional Effects of School-Average Achievement and SES: a Substantive-Methodological Synergy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09726-4
title: The BFLPE model: social comparison processes explain adverse effects of school-average achievement on academic self-concept
description: The BFLPE model hypothesizes that students compare their own achievements with those of classmates and use this social comparison as a basis for forming academic self-concept. The article states "Individual achievement positively predicts ASC (the better I perform, the higher my ASC). In contrast, school-average achievement negatively predicts ASC (the brighter my classmates, the lower my ASC)." The model integrates relative deprivation theory, psychophysical judgment, social judgment, and social comparison theory, and holds that BFLPE size depends substantially on the extent of ability stratification in schools.
requirements: Students must be able to perceive the relative achievement levels of their classmates for social comparison to operate
constraints: If all schools had the same school-average achievement, the BFLPE would disappear
examples: The article applies the model as the theoretical basis for predicting negative compositional effects of school-average achievement in the ELS:2002 analysis (Hypothesis 1).
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Dicke, T., Guo, J., Parker, P. D., & Basarkod, G. (2023). Disentangling the Long-Term Compositional Effects of School-Average Achievement and SES: a Substantive-Methodological Synergy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09726-4

article_title: Context-related changes in academic self concept development: On the long-term persistence of big-fish-little-pond effects
citation: Becker, Michael; Neumann, Marko. (2016). Context-related changes in academic self concept development. On the long-term persistence of big-fish-little-pond effects. Learning and instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2016.06.003
title: Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect (BFLPE) framework of contextual influences on academic self-concept
description: The BFLPE framework holds that academic self-concept develops not only from individual factors but also from contextual characteristics of the learning environment, especially the abilities of classmates. As the article states, "Besides individual factors, contextual characteristics play an important role in driving changes in self-perception", and "The abilities of classmates are especially important". The framework predicts that equally able students form lower ASCs in higher-achieving classrooms, and the article extends it by testing whether the effect persists across consecutive school contexts.
requirements: Contextual information about classmates' achievement in each school context the student passes through
constraints: The article's evidence covers students transitioning from elementary to secondary school; the prior-context effect faded within one year
examples: The study drew on a sample of fourth graders who transitioned from elementary school to secondary school, using contextual information from both settings.
key_sources: Becker, Michael; Neumann, Marko. (2016). Context-related changes in academic self concept development. On the long-term persistence of big-fish-little-pond effects. Learning and instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2016.06.003

article_title: The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: Beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Arens, A. K. (2019). The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111 (2). pp. 331-353. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000281
title: Big-fish-little-pond effect (BFLPE): social comparison effects of school-average achievement on self-concept
description: The BFLPE posits that students form academic self-concepts by comparing their abilities with classmates'. As the article states, 'students in schools that have a high school-average achievement will have lower ASCs than will equally able students in schools where the school-average ability is not high'. The article reviews extensive cross-national support and negative effects on aspirations, grades, and later attendance, and tests whether the effect extends to self-efficacy-like measures.
requirements: School-average achievement as a contextual predictor and individual-level self-belief measures analyzed in multilevel or contextual-effect models
constraints: The article predicts the BFLPE is attenuated or eliminated for pure self-efficacy responses
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept and educational aspiration outcomes
examples: PISA-based reviews cited in the article found negative school-average-achievement effects on academic self-concept in 122 of 123 country samples
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Arens, A. K. (2019). The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111 (2). pp. 331-353. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000281

article_title: Association between the big five personalities and academic performance among grade 12 students at international high school in Thailand.
citation: Korn, B., Gobhathai, S. & Rattanaumpawan, P. (2025). Association between the big five personalities and academic performance among grade 12 students at international high school in Thailand. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-01038-7
title: Big Five Inventory (BFI) 44-item personality assessment questionnaire
description: The Big Five Inventory (BFI) is "a well-established personality assessment tool" and "a 44-item questionnaire that assesses the five personalities attributed to the Big Five Personality". Respondents "rate their agreement with each of the 44 statements on a scale from 'strongly disagree, 0 points' to 'strongly agree, 5 points'", and scores are calculated as the mean for each of the five traits. The article reports previous studies demonstrating its reliability and validity.
requirements: Respondents rate agreement with all 44 statements on a 0–5 scale; scores are averaged per trait
constraints: The article used the English-language version with Grade-12 students at an international high school in Thailand
target_learning_goals: Assessment of the five Big Five personality domains
examples: Used as section 1 of the study questionnaire distributed to all Grade-12 students online or on paper
key_sources: Korn, B., Gobhathai, S. & Rattanaumpawan, P. (2025). Association between the big five personalities and academic performance among grade 12 students at international high school in Thailand. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-01038-7
